4.1 The good-grading conditions. By step 1.3, the centralizer $\mathfrak g^e$ has a homogeneous basis $e_{i,j;r}$ with $r\ge s_{i,j}\ge0$, so it has no negative-degree part. Invariance gives $\operatorname{tr}([e,x]y)=-\operatorname{tr}(x[e,y])$, so the transpose of the map on degree $r$ is, up to sign, $\operatorname{ad}e:\mathfrak g_{-r-1}\to\mathfrak g_{-r}$. 4.2 Dynkin normalization and the zero boundary. Work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ be a partition
of $N\ge0$ with transpose $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, where $l=p_n$ for a
nonempty row list and $l=0$ for an empty row list. Zero-length rows have no
boxes. Let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with matrix units
$e_{i,j}$ in the standard basis
$v_1,\dots,v_N$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]). Number the
boxes of the diagram of $\lambda$ by $1,\dots,N$ down columns from the left,
and for a box $i$ write $\mathrm{row}(i),\mathrm{col}(i)$ for its row and
column, $L(i)$ for the box immediately to its left (or $\emptyset$ if absent),
and $R(i)$ for the box immediately to its right (or $\emptyset$ if absent).
Define the nilpotent endomorphism
$$e=\sum_{i:\ L(i)\ne\emptyset}e_{L(i),i}\in\mathfrak g,\qquad ev_i=v_{L(i)},$$
and declare $\deg e_{i,j}=\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)$ for all $i,j$, so
that $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak g_r$ with
$\mathfrak g_r=\operatorname{span}\{e_{i,j}:\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)=r\}$.
Put
$$\mathfrak p=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r,\qquad \mathfrak h=\mathfrak g_0,\qquad \mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r<0}\mathfrak g_r,$$
and for rows $1\le i,j\le n$ define the shift $s_{i,j}=p_j-p_i$ if $i\le j$
and $s_{i,j}=0$ if $i\ge j$, together with the centralizer elements
$$e_{i,j;r}=\sum_{\substack{\mathrm{row}(h)=i,\ \mathrm{row}(k)=j\\ \mathrm{col}(k)-\mathrm{col}(h)=r}}e_{h,k} \qquad(s_{i,j}\le r<p_j).$$
Finally let $\chi\colon\mathfrak m\to\mathbb C$ be $\chi(x)=\operatorname{tr}(xe)$,
where the trace is the trace of the $N\times N$ matrix.

The verification below records the properties of this data that are used
throughout this page. $e\in\mathfrak g_1$ has Jordan type $\lambda$; $\mathfrak p$
is a parabolic subalgebra with Levi factor
$\mathfrak h\cong\mathfrak{gl}_{q_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_{q_l}$ and
nilradical $\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$, while $\mathfrak m$ is the
nilradical of the opposite parabolic; the elements $e_{i,j;r}$ with
$s_{i,j}\le r<p_j$ form a basis of the centralizer
$\mathfrak g^e=\{X\in\mathfrak g:[X,e]=0\}$; the box set
$J=\{(a,b)\in\{1,\dots,N\}^2:\mathrm{col}(a)\le\mathrm{col}(b),\ R(b)=\emptyset\}$

and $s_{i,j}=0$ if $i\ge j$, together with the centralizer elements
$$e_{i,j;r}=\sum_{\substack{\mathrm{row}(h)=i,\ \mathrm{row}(k)=j\\ \mathrm{col}(k)-\mathrm{col}(h)=r}}e_{h,k} \qquad(s_{i,j}\le r<p_j).$$

All matrix spaces below carry the commutator bracket $[A,B]=AB-BA$ and are
Lie subalgebras of $\mathfrak{gl}_m(\mathbb C)=M_m(\mathbb C)$ in the sense of
[[def-lie-algebra-over-a-field]]; closure under the bracket is verified in
each case by the computation displayed.

* The **general linear Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{gl}_n(\mathbb C)=M_n(\mathbb C)$,
  for $n\ge1$. The **special linear Lie algebra**
  $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb C):\operatorname{tr}A=0\}$
  is a Lie subalgebra because $\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0$, and
  $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ agrees with
  [[def-special-linear-lie-algebra-sl-two]].
* The **symplectic Lie algebra** $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ is the set of
  $A\in M_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ with $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\-I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$.
* The **orthogonal Lie algebras** $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
  $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}(\mathbb C)$ are the sets of $A\in M_m(\mathbb C)$ with
  $AJ+JA^{T}=0$, for $n\ge1$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_n\\I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for
  $m=2n$ and
  $J=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&I_n\\0&I_n&0\end{pmatrix}$ for $m=2n+1$.

$A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&-a^{T}\end{pmatrix}$ for the symplectic and even
orthogonal cases, with $b,c$ symmetric for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$ and
$b,c$ skew-symmetric for $\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)$, and gives

and $\dim\mathfrak{so}_{2n}(\mathbb C)=n(2n-1)$. Each set is closed under the

invariant in the sense that

$$B_\rho([z,x],y)+B_\rho(x,[z,y])=0.$$

definition makes $U(\mathfrak g)$ a unital associative algebra and $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$ a
linear map. It does not assert that $\iota_{\mathfrak g}$ is injective; that conclusion will

$\mathfrak g\times V\to V$ satisfying

$$[x,y]v=x(yv)-y(xv)$$

for all $x,y\in\mathfrak g$ and $v\in V$. No finite-dimensional hypothesis is
imposed on either $\mathfrak g$ or $V$. The zero vector space and the zero
action are allowed.

Consequently $e$ is nilpotent of Jordan type $\lambda=(p_1,\dots,p_n)$, $e\in\mathfrak g_1$, and the number of columns is $l=p_n$ when the row list is nonempty, with $l=0$ for the empty row list. Zero-length rows contribute no Jordan strings; for $N=0$ all box-indexed sums and vector spaces are empty or zero.

Parabolic structure. The degree defines a $\mathbb Z$-grading of the associative algebra: $\deg(e_{h,k}e_{k',l})=\deg e_{h,k}+\deg e_{k',l}$ when $k=k'$ by [F1], and $[\mathfrak g_r,\mathfrak g_s]\subseteq\mathfrak g_{r+s}$. Hence $\mathfrak p=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r$ is a subalgebra, its degree-zero part $\mathfrak h$ consists of the matrices $e_{h,k}$ with $\mathrm{col}(h)=\mathrm{col}(k)$, which is exactly the block-diagonal subalgebra with blocks of sizes $q_1,\dots,q_l$, so $\mathfrak h\cong\mathfrak{gl}_{q_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_{q_l}$; the strictly positive part $\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$ is a nilpotent ideal and $\mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r<0}\mathfrak g_r$ is the nilradical of the opposite parabolic, with $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak m\oplus\mathfrak h\oplus\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$.

The centralizer basis. First $[e,e_{h,k}]=e_{L(h),k}-e_{h,R(k)}$ for boxes $h,k$, with a term omitted when the relevant neighbour is absent (this is $[e,e_{h,k}]=\sum_d(e_{L(d),d}e_{h,k}-e_{h,k}e_{L(d),d})$ and $e_{L(d),d}e_{h,k}=\delta_{d,h}e_{L(d),k}$, while $e_{h,k}e_{L(d),d}=\delta_{L(d),k}e_{h,d}$ and $L(d)=k$ holds exactly for $d=R(k)$ in the same row). Now write $e_{i,j;r}=\sum_ce_{h_c,k_c}$ with $h_c$ the box of row $i$ in column $c$ and $k_c$ the box of row $j$ in column $c+r$, the sum over $c$ with $1\le c\le p_i$ and $1\le c+r\le p_j$; here $r\ge s_{i,j}\ge0$ by the defining range, so this index set is exactly $c=1,\dots,\min(p_i,p_j-r)$. Then $[e,e_{i,j;r}]=\sum_c(e_{h_{c-1},k_c}-e_{h_c,k_{c+1}})$ where a term is omitted when the neighbour does not exist; shifting the second sum by $c\mapsto c+1$ and using $R(k_c)=k_{c+1}$ (which exists exactly when $c+r<p_j$) shows that the two sums run over the same index set $\{c:c\ge2,\ c\le\min(p_i,p_j-r)\}$, because for every $c$ in the defining range one has $c+r\le p_j$; hence the commutator is $0$. The $e_{i,j;r}$ are linearly independent because they are sums over pairwise disjoint matrix units, and their number is $\sum_{i,j}\#\{r:s_{i,j}\le r<p_j\}=\sum_{i,j}(p_j-\max(0,p_j-p_i))=\sum_{i,j}\min(p_i,p_j)$, which equals $\dim\mathfrak g^e$ by [F2]. Hence they form a basis of $\mathfrak g^e$.

The bijection $J\to K$. For $(a,b)\in J$ put $i=\mathrm{row}(a)$, $j=\mathrm{row}(b)$ and $r=\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)$. Because $b$ is rightmost, $\mathrm{col}(b)=p_j$; hence $r=p_j-\mathrm{col}(a)\ge0$, $r<p_j$ because $\mathrm{col}(a)\ge1$, and $r\ge p_j-p_i$ because $\mathrm{col}(a)\le p_i$. Thus $s_{i,j}=\max(0,p_j-p_i)\le r<p_j$, so the map lands in $K$. The triple determines $b$ as the rightmost box of row $j$ and $a$ as the box of row $i$ in column $p_j-r$, proving injectivity. Conversely, if $(i,j,r)\in K$, then $r<p_j$ gives $1\le p_j-r$, while $r\ge\max(0,p_j-p_i)$ gives $p_j-r\le p_i$. Thus those two boxes exist, their columns satisfy $\mathrm{col}(a)\le\mathrm{col}(b)$, and they give the required preimage. If either row has length zero, the index range in $K$ is empty, consistently with the absence of such a box pair.

The character. For $x,y\in\mathfrak m$ one has $[x,y]\in[\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m]\subseteq\mathfrak g_{\le-2}$ by step 1.2, and $e\in\mathfrak g_1$, so $[x,y]e\in\mathfrak g_{\le-1}$ and $\operatorname{tr}([x,y]e)=0$ by [F3]. Hence $\chi([\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m])=0$, that is, $\chi$ is a Lie algebra character on $\mathfrak m$: for $x,y\in\mathfrak m$, $\chi([x,y])=\operatorname{tr}([x,y]e)=0$.

The good-grading conditions. By step 1.3, the centralizer $\mathfrak g^e$ has a homogeneous basis $e_{i,j;r}$ with $r\ge s_{i,j}\ge0$, so it has no negative-degree part. The kernel of $\operatorname{ad}e:\mathfrak g_r\to\mathfrak g_{r+1}$ is $\mathfrak g^e\cap\mathfrak g_r$, hence this map is injective for $r<0$. The trace pairing is nondegenerate between $\mathfrak g_r$ and $\mathfrak g_{-r}$: each matrix unit $e_{a,b}$ pairs with $e_{b,a}$, and matrix units of other total degree have zero trace. Invariance gives $\operatorname{tr}([e,x]y)=-\operatorname{tr}(x[e,y])$, so the transpose of the map on degree $r$ is, up to sign, $\operatorname{ad}e:\mathfrak g_{-r-1}\to\mathfrak g_{-r}$. For $r\ge0$ the latter is injective by the negative-degree result; finite-dimensional duality therefore makes the original map surjective. These are the good-grading conditions for degree-one $e$. They remain valid when $e=0$, because all nonzero spaces then have degree zero.

The identity $\xi_{a,b}=e_{\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b);\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)}$. Left shifts of $a$ run through the boxes of row $i$ in columns $\mathrm{col}(a),\mathrm{col}(a)-1,\dots,1$, and the corresponding left shifts of $b$ run through the boxes of row $j$ in columns $\mathrm{col}(b),\mathrm{col}(b)-1,\dots,\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)+1$; all these exist because $\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)+1\ge1$ and the shifts stop while the row $i$ box exists. The pairs $(\mathrm{row}(h),\mathrm{row}(k))$ obtained are exactly the pairs $(i,j)$ with column difference $\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)$ and $\mathrm{col}(h)$ ranging over $1,\dots,\mathrm{col}(a)$; by step 2.1 these are exactly the pairs indexing $e_{\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b);\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)}$. Hence the two finite sums coincide, and the two displayed families are the same basis of $\mathfrak g^e$.

If $e\ne0$, step 1.1 puts this nonzero element in pyramid degree $1$, whereas the standard Dynkin grading defined by an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple has $[h,e]=2e$ and puts it in degree $2$; these two gradings therefore differ. There is no assertion that every Dynkin matrix degree is even: on Jordan strings of lengths one and two the standard $h$-weights are $0$ and $1,-1$, so matrix units between these strings have odd weights. If $e=0$, no row has length greater than one, since a row of length at least two contributes a distinct nonzero left-shift matrix unit. Hence all boxes lie in the first column or there are none, every matrix unit has pyramid degree zero, and the zero triple gives the trivial Dynkin grading as well. If $N=0$, there are no matrix units or centralizer indices; the parabolic, Levi, opposite nilradical and trace character are zero. Thus the conventions and good-grading conditions cover repeated row lengths, zero-length rows and the empty pyramid without an exclusion.
